opus-5.5.text:
For me, failure isn't really about one bad run or a loss curve that suddenly spikes. Those things happen constantly; they're just part of daily life when you're training large models. If you treat every one of them as a failure, you'd be demoralized every single day.

The way I think about it, a real failure is when you spend a lot of compute and time and come out the other side without understanding *why* things turned out the way they did. If a run doesn't reach the target but you clearly learn something, like your data mixture was off, or the architecture choice doesn't scale the way you assumed, then that's not wasted. It's an expensive experiment, but it's still an experiment that paid off in knowledge.

The failure I'm afraid of is the kind where the model ends up "okay." It hits the benchmarks reasonably well, nobody complains, but it doesn't actually push anything forward, and the team can't say what it would do differently next time. That's worse than a dramatic crash, because a crash forces you to dig in, while a mediocre result lets you fool yourself.

So in practice I'd define failure on two levels. At the technical level, it's when the model doesn't develop the capability we were really betting on, not just a number on a leaderboard. At the team level, it's when we lose the ability to reason clearly about our own decisions, when we start making choices because "that's what everyone else does" instead of because we have evidence. That second one is the more dangerous failure, and honestly it's the one I spend the most energy trying to prevent.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think I'd define it as a single moment where something goes wrong. For me, failure in training a model like this is more about what the loss curve doesn't tell you.

The obvious failures are easy: the loss diverges, the training crashes, you've burned a huge amount of compute and the checkpoint is unusable. Those are painful, but they're honest. You can see them, you can trace them back to a learning rate, a data issue, a numerical instability, and you fix them.

The failures that actually worry me are quieter. The run finishes, the loss looks beautiful, and then you evaluate and the model is simply not better in the ways that matter. Or it's better on benchmarks and worse in actual use. That's a failure of judgment, not a failure of engineering. It usually means that at some point, maybe months earlier, we made a wrong call about data mixture, or about what the architecture should prioritize, and the training just faithfully executed that wrong decision.

So the way I think about it is in layers. First, did we execute the plan correctly? Second, was the plan right? Third, and this is the hardest one, did we learn something from the run that changes what we'd do next time? If we spent all that compute and came out with no new understanding, even if the model is okay, I'd still count that as a kind of failure. Because the next model depends entirely on what we learned from this one.

And honestly, you have to accept that a certain amount of failure is the cost of doing this at all. If every run succeeds, you're probably not being ambitious enough. What's not acceptable is failing in a way you can't explain.

astra-6.text: I would define failure in terms of what we wanted the model to learn. A training run can finish and the loss can go down, but if the model doesn’t improve on the capabilities we care about—or those improvements don’t generalize beyond the training data—then it hasn’t achieved its goal. I’d distinguish that from a failed experiment, though. If the result helps us identify a wrong assumption and decide what to change next, the experiment still has value.

sol-6.1.text: I would define failure in terms of the goal of the training, rather than a single loss value. If the loss goes down but the ET model doesn’t learn the behavior we want, or that behavior doesn’t generalize to held-out examples, then I would consider that a failed run. A run with disappointing results can still be useful if it tells us clearly what went wrong.
